Empirical Research Plan  
“Roads and Congestion in U.S. Metropolitan Areas, 1983-2003”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Two-stage least squares (panel IV) complemented by an event-study on the instrumented treatment.

Why IV?  
• Road construction is highly endogenous to current or anticipated traffic. OLS or simple DID would bias estimates upward (reverse causality).  
• The original 1947 (general) and 1955 (official) Interstate Highway System blueprints allocated exact corridor mileages to every metropolitan area according to military and political considerations, largely unrelated to post-1980 urban traffic.  
• These blueprints provide a time-invariant, plausibly exogenous “potential road stock.” Interacting that potential with the annual national Interstate construction budget yields a Bartik-type (shift-share) instrument that (a) varies over time, (b) is predetermined, and (c) is powerful (large first-stage F).  

Equation system  
First stage:  
Ln LaneKM_it = α_i + γ_t + β₁ Bartik_it + β₂ X_it + ε_it¹  

Second stage:  
Ln VKT_it = α_i + γ_t + θ Ŷ_it + β₂ X_it + ε_it²  
where Ŷ_it = predicted Ln LaneKM_it from stage 1, α_i = metro FE, γ_t = year FE, X_it = controls (population, GDP, gasoline price, etc.).

An event-study on the IV-predicted lane growth will trace dynamic effects relative to construction years.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (continuous):  
T_it ≡ Ln (Lane-km of limited-access roads in metro i, year t). We will also scale by population (per-capita) in robustness checks.

Control group / counterfactual:  
All metros in the panel serve mutually as controls; identification comes from differential exposure to the national construction shock given their fixed “Interstate blueprint share.” Metros with low blueprint mileage act as implicit controls for those with high mileage.

Treatment timing:  
Annual; the Bartik instrument varies because each year’s national investment share (ΔNational Interstate LaneKM_t / National Blueprint LaneKM) multiplies each metro’s pre-set blueprint stock. No single cutoff—staggered continuous exposure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance (first-stage strength): Blueprint mileage interacted with national spending strongly predicts actual lane-km additions. Plausible—Congress funds projects drawn from the original maps.

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on metro and year FE plus controls, the blueprint-based Bartik shock affects congestion only through actual lane construction, not through any other channel (e.g., local economic shocks). Military/political siting in the 1940s–50s supports this.

A3. Parallel (or “equal-trend”) for IV event study: In absence of treatment, metros with high vs. low blueprint exposure would have had similar traffic trends after conditioning on FE/trends.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-metro spillovers): A lane built in metro i mainly affects traffic inside i. We test for spillovers by adding neighboring-metro lane growth.

A5. Measurement accuracy: Lane-km and VKT are consistently measured across metros/years.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigations  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Violation of exclusion via correlated economic growth  
   • Add metro-year economic controls (GDP, employment, fuel price).  
   • Show balance: blueprint mileage uncorrelated with 1940/1950 population growth, industrial mix.  
   • Placebo test: Re-estimate for pre-Interstate period (1950-1960) when no construction occurred—coefficient should be zero.

T2. Anticipatory or lobbying effects (local demand influencing which blueprint links were actually built)  
   • By using the total blueprint mileage—not only actually completed segments—the instrument is predetermined.  
   • Drop the largest lobbying metros (e.g., DC, LA) in robustness.

T3. Spatial spillovers  
   • Include mileage growth in adjacent metros as a control.  
   • Cluster standard errors by state or 2-digit FIPS to allow for spillover-induced correlation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # Fast data handling
library(fixest)       # High-performance FE and IV
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("hpms_1983_2003.csv")          # main panel
blueprint <- fread("interstate_blueprint_1955.csv") # pre-determined miles
natSpend  <- fread("national_interstate_spend.csv") # yearly totals

# 2. Merge & construct variables ---------------------------------
dt <- merge(dt, blueprint, by = "metro_id")
dt <- merge(dt, natSpend,  by = "year")

# Bartik instrument: (national annual lane km added / national blueprint) * metro blueprint
dt[, bartik := (nat_lane_added / nat_blueprint_lane) * blueprint_lane]

# Key vars
dt[, ln_lane := log(lane_km)]
dt[, ln_vkt  := log(vehicle_km_traveled)]
dt[, ln_pop  := log(population)]

# 3. Baseline IV specification -----------------------------------
iv_formula <- ln_vkt ~ ln_pop + gas_price + gdp_per_capita | 
                         ln_pop + gas_price + gdp_per_capita + bartik

est_iv <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt,
                fixef = ~ metro_id + year,
                cluster = ~ metro_id)

summary(est_iv)

# 4. Event-study on instrumented lanes ---------------------------
# First get residualized treatment
dt[, ln_lane_hat := fitfeols(feols(ln_lane ~ 1 | metro_id + year | bartik, data = dt))]

# Create relative year to first large lane shock (>10% rise)
dt <- dt[order(metro_id, year)]
dt[, treat_start := year[which.max(cumsum(lag(ln_lane, 1, default = ln_lane[1]) - ln_lane) < -0.10)], by = metro_id]
dt[, rel_year := year - treat_start]

# Bin endpoints ±6 years
dt[rel_year < -6, rel_year := -6]
dt[rel_year >  6, rel_year :=  6]

# Event-study regression
es <- feols(ln_vkt ~ i(rel_year, ref = -1, drop = 0) | metro_id + year,
            data = dt, cluster = ~ metro_id,
            iv = ~ ln_lane_hat)

iplot(es) + theme_bw()

# 5. Robustness: drop top-5 blueprint metros ---------------------
top5 <- blueprint[order(-blueprint_lane)][1:5, metro_id]
robust <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt[!metro_id %in% top5],
                fixef = ~ metro_id + year, cluster = ~ metro_id)
summary(robust)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory on “induced demand” predicts an elasticity of VKT with respect to lane-km close to 1. I anticipate θ ≈ 0.8–1.2. A coefficient near 1 implies that, on average, expanding road capacity fully offsets the intended congestion relief—traffic increases proportionally.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (0/1)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Strong first stage (F > 10) ............. 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction credible .......... 0.7  
C3: No spillovers / SUTVA .................... 0.6  
C4: Correct functional form & controls ...... 0.9  
C5: Robust to alternative instruments/trends  0.8  

Average ≈ 0.8 → Generally credible but not bullet-proof; special attention to exclusion and spillovers is required in robustness work.
